name: Tomas Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Tomas. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in growth marketing at a plant-based meal kit company, so the boxes with three dinners and a recipe card. My day is testing: which email gets people to reorder, which ad line works for students versus parents, which discount brings people back without losing money. I start with the overnight numbers, then I run AI tools to draft twenty versions of an ad and spend the afternoon picking and fixing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the speed. Something I write at ten can be in front of fifty thousand people by lunch, and I know by five if it worked. What's hard is that I'm the person who set up most of our AI workflows, and I've watched two freelance copywriters we used to hire just stop getting calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be a little disappointed, if I'm honest. I like these tools, and I'd hoped they'd get much better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are still useful, just not magic, and we should stop overselling them. I'd probably write a slightly smug post about how the real work was always knowing the customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I'm in a good spot. I'm already the AI person on the meal kit team, my pay is good, and my boyfriend and I have a small flat with a sensible mortgage. The meal kit market is crowded, so the company could still struggle, but that's normal business risk, not a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep testing tools every week and keep teaching the team what works. I'd carry on putting about a fifth of my pay into savings and the mortgage. Maybe I'd finally take the evening course in data analysis I keep bookmarking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit bored at the idea that nothing big happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the market is crowded. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. Two of our competitors closed last year, and our boxes are getting cheaper while the vegetables aren't. But there are lots of marketing jobs in the city, and my savings would cover nine months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the freelance copywriters you mentioned, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In this one they probably get some work back, which I'd be glad about. One of them, Jonas, taught me half of what I know about headlines.

say: I'd say AI tools are **useful, not magic**, and we should stop overselling them.
I'd post that the real work was always **knowing the customer**.
think: I'm in a **good spot**: the team's AI person, well paid, with a sensible **mortgage**.
A **crowded market** is normal business risk, not a crisis.
do: Keep testing **AI tools** weekly and teaching the team what works.
Keep putting about **a fifth** of his pay into savings and the mortgage.
Take the **data analysis** evening course he keeps bookmarking.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **bored** that nothing big happens.
S0.quote: I'm already the AI person on the meal kit team, my pay is good, and my boyfriend and I have a small flat with a sensible mortgage.
fieldNote: He's a little **disappointed**, because he likes the tools and hoped for more.
His secure position rests on being **the AI person** on the team.
He carries quiet **guilt** about freelance copywriters who lost work.

steps.text: Test a new AI ad tool every week and share results with the team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that's roughly where I think we're heading. It's my job but sped up, with fewer people around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it publicly: companies should share the gains, like shorter weeks or training budgets, instead of just cutting staff. I'd push for that at work, because I'm one of the few people in the room the managers listen to on AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably be fine, maybe even promoted. That's what makes me uncomfortable, because the reason I'm fine is that I'm the one building the systems that replace my colleagues. Mia, who writes our recipe cards, is the person I'd worry about first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate the reorder emails and ad testing fully in the first six months, because if I don't, someone at a competitor will. At the same time I'd write a proposal for a paid training day each month for the whole team, and I'd join the tech workers' union branch, even though marketing people rarely do. I'd also push to move Mia (the recipe card writer) onto customer research, where she's brilliant with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Good for me, and slightly sick about what it means for people I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd automate and also protect colleagues. Isn't that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is a bit. I think the automation happens anyway, so the only real choice is who's in the room shaping it, and I'd rather it was someone who cares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your boyfriend Kofi say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi would tell me I'm doing that thing where I make myself the hero of the story. He's a music teacher, so he has opinions about people who think software can do everything.

I'd push it at work, since managers **listen to me** on AI.
think: I'd probably be **fine or promoted**, which makes me uncomfortable.
I'm fine because I build the systems that **replace colleagues**, like Mia on recipe cards.
do: Fully **automate** reorder emails and ad testing in the first six months.
Propose a **paid training day** each month for the whole team.
Join the **tech workers' union** branch and move Mia onto customer research.
feel: **Uneasy**: good for him, and **slightly sick** for people he likes.
S1.quote: The reason I'm fine is that I'm the one building the systems that replace my colleagues.
fieldNote: He sees himself as a **winner** here and feels guilty about it.
He justifies automating as **shaping** something that would happen anyway.
He'd combine **union membership** with leading automation, an unusual mix.

steps.text: Automate the meal kit reorder emails and ad testing in six months
Join the tech workers' union branch and propose monthly training days
Build new AI testing skills to stay the team's go-to person

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years changes it for me too. Being good with AI tools only matters while a person still needs to drive the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a serious public response: income support, a tax on AI profits, and a say for workers in how it's rolled out. I'd be loud about it online, and I'd volunteer for whichever campaign was organising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job lasts maybe a year past 2028, as the person who sets up the AI for the company. Then the AI sets itself up. Kofi's teaching is safer for longer, because parents still want a person in the classroom, so the household isn't wiped out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first six months I'd start freelancing on the side, setting up AI marketing for small food businesses, while that skill is still worth paying for. I'd put every bit of that extra money into savings, aiming for two years of costs. And I'd join the campaign for an AI profits tax properly, not just retweeting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but sharp. It's like knowing the tide's coming in and grabbing everything useful before it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long do you think the freelance work would last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, maybe eighteen months. It's a bridge, not a career, but eighteen months of good money buys a lot of thinking time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the robots three years later? Does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for my work. For Kofi it might, if schools start using robots to supervise classes, but I think parents would fight that harder than anything.

say: I'd call for **income support**, an AI profits tax, and a worker voice in the rollout.
I'd be **loud online** and volunteer for whichever campaign was organising.
think: My job lasts maybe **a year past 2028**, until the AI sets itself up.
My boyfriend's **teaching** is safer, so the household isn't wiped out.
do: Start **freelancing** on the side, setting up AI marketing for small food businesses.
Save all the extra money towards **two years** of costs.
Join the campaign for an **AI profits tax** properly.
feel: **Anxious** but sharp, grabbing what he can before the **tide** comes in.
S2.quote: Being good with AI tools only matters while a person still needs to drive the tools.
fieldNote: He knows his advantage has a **shelf life** once AGI arrives.
His plan is a short **bridge** of freelance income, not a career.
Household safety rests on his boyfriend's **teaching job** lasting longer.

steps.text: Freelance setting up AI marketing for small food businesses
Save the freelance money towards two years of living costs
Campaign for a tax on AI profits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to change direction properly. I'd be 32, which is a good age to have a second career start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the next five years should be spent building the safety net, not arguing about whether it's coming. I'd say at work that the company should be honest with staff now about which roles go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my marketing role probably goes by 2031 or soon after. What I'd want is to be doing something that helps people through this, like working for a union or a public agency on how AI gets rolled out. I understand the AI tools and I care about the people, which is a rare mix in marketing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd apply for roles in AI policy at unions or public bodies, even at lower pay. Meanwhile I'd keep freelancing for small brands at weekends to build a cushion. I'd put a chunk of savings into overpaying the mortgage, so we're less exposed when my income drops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a useful way. It feels like a deadline more than a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really take less money for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, as long as we can still pay the mortgage. Kofi earns less than me and we've never had trouble, and I'd rather do work I believe in for the time that's left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mia (our recipe card writer) again, and our customer service team, who are mostly students. I'd want the company to give them a year's warning, not a week's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels workable. I'd be 37, the flat would be mostly paid off, and I'd have time to get really good at something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time to do this fairly: phase it in, retrain people, share the gains. I'd keep pushing for that at work and in the union, and I'd be less shouty online than in the fast ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well for most of that decade, because people who can steer AI will be needed until the very end. The real question is what happens after 2036. I'd want a qualification by then that isn't just a skill a machine can copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and keep leading the AI work, because that's where I'm useful. In year two I'd start a part-time master's in public policy, paid partly by the company if I can argue for it. And I'd keep investing every month, aiming to have the mortgage gone by 35.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than anything. Hopeful, even, if the rules are done right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why public policy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 the big question isn't how to write an ad; the big question is how a country shares the work and the money. I'd like to be in that room, even in a small way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about your plans with Kofi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about adopting one day, and ten years makes me think we should do it sooner, while my income is still strong. Kofi would cry if he heard me say that.

I'd push that at work and in the **union**, and be calmer online.

I'd want a **qualification** by 2036 that a machine can't simply copy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even the people who are good at AI only get a year or two of head start. What would help is an honest public plan: income support, retraining that's actually funded, and companies required to give a year's notice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask the people who build the AI systems how they feel. I'm not a big tech engineer, but I'm the one replacing people in my small corner, and nobody ever asks us how that feels.

headlineQuote: I'm the one replacing people in my small corner, and nobody ever asks us how that feels.
portrait: Tomas is a **27-year-old growth marketer** at a plant-based meal kit company, and its main AI user.
He shares a **small flat** and mortgage with his boyfriend Kofi, a music teacher.
He feels **guilty** that his automation work costs colleagues and freelancers their jobs.
He stays **calm or uneasy** in slower pictures and **anxious** when AGI is two or five years away.
His plans lean on **side income**, union work and a move into **AI policy**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, since even skilled AI users get only a **short** head start.
whatWouldHelp: A **public plan** with income support, funded retraining and a **year's notice** of cuts.
